stem: Your workload is a set of independent circuits with no feedback between them. A colleague suggests always using a session 'to be safe'. According to IBM's guidance, why is batch usually the better default here?

options.text: Batch mode guarantees your jobs run before any other user's jobs.
A session can hold only one job at a time, so a set of independent circuits would have to be spread across many separate sessions, one per circuit.
Sessions cost more than batches, so batch is generally the better choice unless you need the exclusive access that only a session provides.
Sessions do not support the SamplerV2 and EstimatorV2 primitives.
Batch mode transpiles your circuits to the ISA for you before they are queued, whereas inside a session you must supply already-transpiled circuits yourself.
A session has to be closed and reopened between primitive calls, so a set of independent circuits would pay the session start-up cost once per circuit.

explanation.correct: Sessions provide dedicated, exclusive access but at higher usage cost. The docs recommend using batch whenever you don't need that dedicated access — as with a set of independent jobs — because batch delivers the same parallel classical processing and single queue wait more cheaply.

distractors.A: Batch jobs do not get priority over other users; they are not even exclusive. It is sessions that reserve the QPU.
distractors.B: Sessions are explicitly designed for multi-job workloads: one session runs many jobs back-to-back, so nothing forces one session per circuit.
distractors.D: Both primitives run in sessions (and in batches and job mode); the mode is passed via `mode=`.
distractors.E: Neither mode transpiles for you: every execution mode requires ISA circuits produced by a preset pass manager. The choice between batch and session is about scheduling and cost, never about who does the transpilation.
distractors.F: A session stays open across many primitive calls — that is the entire point of the dedicated window. Nothing forces a close between calls; the real cost argument is that the dedicated window itself is billed more than a batch.
